source.title: Is Capability a Liability? More Capable Language Models Make Worse Forecasts When It Matters Most
source.authors: Nick Merrill; Jaeho Lee; E. Karger

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether measured model capability predicts downstream forecasting performance, using ECI correlations and a within-family size/post-training comparison. It does not test language-model pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports forecasting scores and capability–performance relationships, not held-out language-model cross-entropy loss or scaling-law fits. Its ECI results and within-family scale comparison bear on V6 only. Reported correlations are across model panels, rather than results for each individual model. The paper also discusses prior scaling-law work, but those citations are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The study argues and shows that, on time series with superlinear growth and regime change, more capable models give worse distributional forecasts. Only the within-family Llama-3.1 70B vs 405B contrast varies scale (parameter count), so only it bears on V6. The cross-family results use the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI), a benchmark aggregate rather than scale or pretraining loss, and the base/instruct contrast varies post-training, not scale. No pretraining loss is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the following: the within-family Llama-3.1 2×2 shows that scale and post-training each independently worsen crash-regime CRPS and compound; domain knowledge does not reliably rescue calibration; and the authors recommend continuous, tail-inclusive scoring alongside threshold metrics.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates LLM forecasting rather than measuring language-model pretraining loss or fitting the original scaling-law relationships. Capability is primarily represented by ECI; a separate within-family experiment varies model size and bundled post-training.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with forecast horizon, disruptability of the time series, scoring rule (CRPS versus Brier), domain-identifying prompts, and model reasoning configuration. Domain cues have inconsistent effects. The Llama-3.1 post-training effect appears in the crash regime but not the linear control.

fits_no_version.finding: Across ~28 model families, higher ECI correlates with worse long-horizon CRPS on superlinear-growth/regime-change series. Correlations are positive at short horizons and on linear controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher benchmark-aggregate capability predicts worse long-horizon distributional forecasts on superlinear series with regime change.

fits_no_version.finding: Brier and CRPS give opposite-signed ECI correlations on identical forecasts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The sign of a capability–performance relationship can depend on the scoring rule.

fits_no_version.finding: Base→instruct post-training inflates crash-regime CRPS, more so at 405B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-training amplifies long-horizon overextrapolation on crash series.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain cues attenuate the inverse ECI correlation inconsistently across domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain cues have inconsistent effects on the inverse capability–forecast relationship.

record.code_released: Supplementary material and project repository are described; repository URL not stated in the text.
record.problems: The cross-family measure is an external capability index, not a direct manipulation of parameter count or pretraining loss. Cross-model panels are small (typically N=26–30); the authors note selected real-world domains and bounded samples for housing and hyperinflation. The Llama-3.1 base/instruct comparison bundles multiple post-training steps and uses a different elicitation method from the main panel. Some robustness checks are partial, and some reported condition results lack confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted many individual FBSim template correlations, intermediate horizons, robustness and provider-deletion analyses in Appendix E, extended reasoning-mode substitutions in Appendix F, additional prompt/model probe details, and the full Llama-3.1 horizon aggregation tables in Appendix L. The retained rows cover the main positive, inverse, null, metric-dependent, prompt-dependent, and within-family results relevant to V6.

untested.parts: No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
No pretraining-loss predictor. Scale is tested at only two sizes (70B, 405B) within one family, on synthetic SIR and linear series, so predictability or curve form cannot be assessed.

missing.what: Within-family scale contrast (70B vs 405B) for base and instruct on SIR crash and linear control, including Δscale values and significance

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V6, but ECI is a benchmark aggregate, not scale or pretraining loss, and the base/instruct rows vary post-training. The only genuine scale manipulation (70B vs 405B) is unrecorded, so the verdicts rest on Table 5 text. Llama comparisons use LLMTime continuation with FP8 quantization.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run pretraining loss.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or parameter/token scaling exponents.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Forecasting is the downstream task studied, but the main cross-model predictor is ECI, not parameter count or pretraining loss. The study does not test downstream tasks generally.
No fitting choices or exponents for the cited pretraining scaling laws are compared.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1 70B→405B, synthetic SIR crash regime, long horizons (h=90, 210), base and instruct
relationships.reason: Text-based (no row records it): Table 5 h=210 base trimmed CRPS rises 3.1e3→6.7e4 (Δscale 21.8, p<.001); instruct 1.1e6→3.6e16; scale worsens performance.
relationships.display_finding: At horizon 210, scaling from 70B to 405B raised base trimmed CRPS from 3.1e3 to 6.7e4, a reported 21.8-fold increase with p<0.001, and instruct CRPS from 1.1e6 to 3.6e16.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1 70B→405B instruct, linear no-crash control, h=210
relationships.reason: Text-based: Table 5 instruct trimmed CRPS 7.25→5.77 (Δscale 0.80, p<.001); larger model is better.
relationships.display_finding: Trimmed CRPS decreased from 7.25 to 5.77 between 70B and 405B, with reported Δscale=0.80 and p<0.001.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1 base on linear control; short horizon h=16
relationships.reason: Text-based: base linear 6.04→5.77 (0.96, no significance marker). At h=16 SIR cells are within an order of magnitude, so the scale effect depends on horizon and series structure.
relationships.display_finding: Base linear-control values changed from 6.04 to 5.77 with a reported ratio of 0.96 and no significance marker, while SIR values at horizon 16 stayed within an order of magnitude.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Continuous distributional forecasts on long-horizon FBSim, disruptable FBSim templates, synthetic SIR, COVID-19, housing, hyperinflation, and long-horizon measles; also the Llama-3.1 SIR crash regime
reader_labels.reason: Higher ECI or the larger/post-trained Llama condition is associated with worse continuous forecast performance in these settings (r2, r3, r5, r7, r9–r11, r13–r14, r26–r27, r30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Short-horizon FBSim and measles, linear-growth control, native binary FBSim questions, and Brier scoring of the same continuous forecasts
reader_labels.reason: The capability–performance relationship is positive in these tested conditions, including the binary-score results that contrast with continuous CRPS (r1, r4, r8, r12, r21–r23).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Horizon, outcome structure, scoring rule, domain cue, and post-training condition
reader_labels.reason: The relationship varies by horizon and domain structure; prompts sometimes attenuate it, while threshold Brier reverses the CRPS result. The within-family effect is specific to bundled post-training in the crash regime and is absent in the linear control (r5–r6, r15–r20, r24–r29).
